land.text: the same territory, under the unitary and centralist constitution of 1886

predecessors.note: Cliopatria's Republic of Colombia row begins in 1866 on the same outline; the page puts the new name in 1886.

correction.text: the 1866 outline, valid for 1886 to the secession of Panama on 3 November 1903

keyframe_review.note: Cliopatria draws this shape from 1866, but the page has the United States of Colombia (created in 1863) 'known as the Republic of Colombia in 1886' ('before finally adopting its present name - the Republic of Colombia - in 1886'): 1866-1885 belong to the united-states-of-colombia dossier (new keyframe 1866-1886 there) and the shape stands here for 1886-1903 only. 1.223 M km2 includes Panama (282 cells, 71,318 km2) and the border cells; without Panama 1.152 M km2 against the infobox 1,141,748 km2 (undated; ratio 1.009).

New keyframe 1904: 'The secession of Panama from Colombia was formalized on 3 November 1903', but Cliopatria's shape without Panama begins in 1905 (the 1866 shape runs to 1904). Colombia without the Department of Panama is the 1905 shape. Panama had been 'the Department of the Isthmus' under centralism and 'the Panama Department of Colombia' from 1886.

1.140 M km2, the 1866 outline minus the 282 Panama cells (71,318 km2). Against the infobox 1,141,748 km2 the ratio is 1.00. The shape omits the Amazon trapezium of Leticia (37 cells, 9,357 km2), which comes in 1928, and the San Andrés archipelago (the page names it as a Colombian archipelago; at 52 km2 it is below the grid).

1.150 M km2 (+9,357 km2 against 1905): Leticia enters with the 1928 ratification of the 1922 agreement ('despite the treaty's ratification in 1928'), plus 3 cells from Brazil on the Apaporis (1928 Brazil-Colombia treaty). Infobox 1,141,748 km2 (ratio 1.007). The shape holds through the Peruvian seizure of 1932 and the League award of June 1934, which is a contest, not a change of owner. The 31 Peruvian, 11 Ecuadorian, 13 Venezuelan and 11 Brazilian cells inside the shape are grid fuzz along the rivers, as in 1905.

Unchanged from 1928; the page lists the frontiers (Panama, Venezuela, Brazil, Ecuador, Peru) and 'seven agreements on the Caribbean Sea and three on the Pacific Ocean' without dates. The page does not mention the 2012 ICJ case on San Andrés; the archipelago is below the grid.

region.text: the whole country including Panama, as the United States of Colombia held it

ledger.note: 1886: Colombia becomes the Republic of Colombia, a centralised republic. 'which became known as the Republic of Colombia in 1886'; 'before finally adopting its present name - the Republic of Colombia - in 1886'. The page gives no month; the same state as the United States of Colombia (that dossier ends in 1886).

region.text: the Department of Panama, the Isthmus

ledger.note: 3 November 1903: Panama separates. 'The secession of Panama from Colombia was formalized on 3 November 1903'; the Tiradores Battalion 'arrived in the Panamanian city of Colón the morning of November 3, 1903' under Generals Juan Tovar and Ramón Amaya and the USS Nashville had landed on 2 November; the United States formally recognised Panama on 13 November 1903 and the Hay-Bunau-Varilla Treaty was signed on 18 November. Colombia recognised Panama 'in 1909, after receiving a US$500,000' payment by one passage and under the Thomson-Urrutia Treaty of 1921 by another.

region.text: the Leticia district, the Amazon trapezium

ledger.note: 1928: Leticia passes to Colombia. In 1922 the two governments 'reached a controversial agreement awarding the Leticia area to Colombia', in exchange 'for recognizing Peru's rights to the zone south of the' Putumayo; the page gives the ratification as 1928 and no handover date. The Colombia-Peru War page dates the 'Boundary Treaty of March 24, 1922' (the Salomón-Lozano treaty page would not load). Cliopatria draws 37 cells (9,357 km2).

region.text: the 3 cells on the Apaporis-Amazon segment

ledger.note: 1928: the Tratado de Límites y Navegación Fluvial fixes the Apaporis-Amazon segment with Brazil; Cliopatria passes 3 cells (759 km2) near the Apaporis to Colombia. The page gives no areas and no date for the earlier Vásquez Cobo-Martins treaty.

region.text: the Leticia district, the Amazon trapezium

ledger.note: 1 September 1932: Peruvian civilians and soldiers seize Leticia. 'In the early hours of September 1, 1932, what is now known as the Leticia Incident took place after Leticia was seized by Peruvian soldiers'; Peru sent two regiments to Leticia and Tarapacá and its forces encamped on the Putumayo.

region.text: the Leticia district, the Amazon trapezium

ledger.note: June 1934: the Leticia contest ends. 'The League finally awarded the disputed area to Colombia in June 1934' after the war (1 September 1932 to 24 May 1933 on the Colombia-Peru War page) and a League of Nations commission; the Rio de Janeiro Protocol of 1934 followed. The Colombia-Peru War page says 'an agreement was reached to divide the disputed area'.

wars.name: Thousand Days' War
wars.outcome: The page names it 'the most significant' of the civil wars; 'between 100 and 180 thousand Colombians lost their lives'. It gives no outcome, territory or treaty.
wars.note: No zone recorded: the page is silent on what the rebels held; Panama's separation followed the war by a year. A gap-filler should open the war's own page.

wars.name: Colombia-Peru War

zones.text: the Leticia district, the Amazon trapezium

wars.outcome: The war 'lasted from September 1, 1932, to May 24, 1933'; the League of Nations commission took Leticia, and the League awarded the disputed area to Colombia in June 1934 (Rio de Janeiro Protocol, 1934).
wars.note: Rooted in the Boundary Treaty of March 24, 1922. Peru's forces 'encamped on the banks of the Putumayo River'.

certainty.note: The Amazon frontiers with Peru, Ecuador and Brazil are disputed until the 1922 treaty, the Brazilian treaties and the Leticia settlement; the Panama frontier is administrative until the secession of 1903.

The Peruvian frontier follows the 1922 treaty (ratified 1928) and the 1934 Rio Protocol, the Brazilian segment the 1928 treaty; the Venezuelan, Ecuadorian and Panamanian frontiers are not covered by the pages opened and stay as Cliopatria draws them.

notes: Cliopatria's Republic of Colombia row (1866-2024) starts twenty years before the name: the United States of Colombia dossier (am-08) keeps 1863-1886 and carries a new keyframe 1866-1886, so this dossier starts in 1886 and reviews the 1866 shape as valid from 1886. Panama leaves on 3 November 1903 (split; Cliopatria's shape without Panama starts in 1905, so a new keyframe holds 1904). Page failed: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sal%C3%B3mon%E2%80%93Lozano_Treaty and the hyphen spelling both returned URL_NOT_FOUND; the 1922 treaty and its 1928 ratification are taken from the Colombia-Peru War and Leticia pages (the handover date of 1930 is on neither). Disagreements: Colombia's recognition of Panama is 1909 (one passage) or 1921 (Thomson-Urrutia); the Colombia page gives the Panama seizure as 1903 with US backing; the war ends 24 May 1933 (page) while the League award is June 1934. Not covered (page budget 5 of 5, the Brazil-Colombia page reused from the Brazil dossier): the Thousand Days' War outcome and its Panama zone, the 1907 Brazil treaty date, the San Andrés and Providencia archipelago (Esguerra-Bárcenas, 1928; the ICJ 2012), Los Monjes, the Venezuelan frontier (1891 arbitration, 1941), the Ecuadorian frontier, the Panamanian frontier treaty, Quitasueño and Serrana. The Cliopatria shape contains 31 Peruvian, 11 Ecuadorian, 13 Venezuelan and 11 Brazilian border cells (grid fuzz, not claims). Counterparts: republic-of-panama and republic-of-peru (am-08), brazilian-republic (this part), united-states-of-colombia (am-08). Rulers omitted.
